JavaScript.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
options: A function that retains access to variables in its outer lexical scope even after that outer function has returned
A method to terminate an infinite loop in asynchronous callbacks
A function that executes immediately and deletes all enclosed local variables
A special syntax for defining private variables in ES5 constructor functions only
JavaScript.correct_answer: A function that retains access to variables in its outer lexical scope even after that outer function has returned

JavaScript.question: How does an arrow function handle the 'this' keyword compared to a standard function declaration?
options: It inherits 'this' lexically from the surrounding scope at the time it is defined
It binds 'this' dynamically to the element or object that invokes it
It automatically binds 'this' to the global window object in strict mode
It creates its own fresh execution context for 'this' upon every invocation
JavaScript.correct_answer: It inherits 'this' lexically from the surrounding scope at the time it is defined

JavaScript.question: When an 'await' expression is evaluated inside an async function, what actually happens?
options: It pauses the execution of the async function until the Promise settles, while leaving the main thread unblocked
It halts the entire browser JavaScript runtime until the network request completes synchronously
It converts the asynchronous Promise into a synchronous blocking system thread
It forces the immediate rejection of any pending microtasks in the event loop
JavaScript.correct_answer: It pauses the execution of the async function until the Promise settles, while leaving the main thread unblocked

JavaScript.question: In the JavaScript Event Loop, which queue takes priority when the call stack clears?
options: Microtask queue (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval)
Macrotask queue (setTimeout) before the microtask queue
Both queues are processed in strict alternating round-robin order
Tasks are picked purely at random based on CPU availability
JavaScript.correct_answer: Microtask queue (Promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) before the macrotask queue (setTimeout, setInterval)

JavaScript.question: In the loop `for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) { setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 10); }`, why does it log 3 three times, and how do closures with 'let' fix this?
options: var is function-scoped so all callbacks close over the same shared variable; 'let' creates a new lexical binding for each loop iteration
setTimeout always caches the final argument value regardless of scope
var is hoisted to global memory while let prevents setTimeout from executing asynchronously
The callbacks run before the loop finishes, so let adds a synchronous delay
JavaScript.correct_answer: var is function-scoped so all callbacks close over the same shared variable; 'let' creates a new lexical binding for each loop iteration

React.question: What is the primary rule when calling React Hooks like useState or useEffect?
options: They must be called at the top level of React function components, not inside loops, conditions, or nested functions
They can only be invoked inside class components' render methods
They must always be passed an async callback function
They should be called inside try/catch blocks for safety
React.correct_answer: They must be called at the top level of React function components, not inside loops, conditions, or nested functions

React.question: What is the purpose of the dependency array in useEffect?
options: It tells React to re-run the effect only when specified values change between renders
It declares the child components that this effect can access
It prevents the component from rendering until all dependencies resolve
It lists the CSS classes that should be injected into the DOM
React.correct_answer: It tells React to re-run the effect only when specified values change between renders

React.question: Why does React use a Virtual DOM?
options: To compute minimal differences (diffing) and batch updates to the real DOM for better rendering performance
To replace the browser DOM entirely and eliminate HTML parsing
To run backend Node.js code directly inside the browser window
To encrypt component state before storing it in localStorage
React.correct_answer: To compute minimal differences (diffing) and batch updates to the real DOM for better rendering performance

Node.js.question: What architecture allows Node.js to handle high concurrency despite running on a single main thread?
options: An event-driven, non-blocking I/O model powered by the libuv event loop and thread pool
Creating a new operating system process for each incoming HTTP request
Synchronous multi-threading through the V8 virtual machine
Automated compile-time parallelism of JavaScript bytecode
Node.js.correct_answer: An event-driven, non-blocking I/O model powered by the libuv event loop and thread pool

Node.js.question: In Express.js, what does calling `next()` inside a middleware function do?
options: Passes control to the next middleware or route handler in the application stack
Immediately terminates the HTTP response and sends a 200 status
Restarts the server process to prevent memory leaks
Redirects the client to the next available route
Node.js.correct_answer: Passes control to the next middleware or route handler in the application stack

Node.js.question: What is the difference between `fs.readFile` and `fs.readFileSync` in Node.js?
options: `fs.readFile` is asynchronous and non-blocking via callback/promises, whereas `fs.readFileSync` blocks the event loop until the file is read
`fs.readFile` can only read text files, while `fs.readFileSync` reads binary data
`fs.readFile` reads from memory cache, whereas `fs.readFileSync` reads from disk
There is no difference; `fs.readFileSync` is just an alias for backwards compatibility
Node.js.correct_answer: `fs.readFile` is asynchronous and non-blocking via callback/promises, whereas `fs.readFileSync` blocks the event loop until the file is read
